Meet Jim Brewer
WAREHOUSES/NIGHTLIFE/LIVE MUSIC/COMMUNITY
01 / THE MAN WITH A VISION

Jim Brewer.
He saw what
Bricktown could be.

FEBRUARY 6, 1937 – NOVEMBER 11, 2008

Before the canal, the crowds, and the festivals, there were old warehouses—and people willing to take a chance on them.

Raised in south Oklahoma City, Jim D. Brewer worked in transmissions, nightclubs, and the oil business before investing in downtown real estate. His family’s obituary remembers an entrepreneur who helped turn overlooked buildings into a destination. [2]

Bricktown’s revival involved many people. Neal Horton’s early preservation work, followed by investors including Jim Tolbert, Don Karchmer, and Brewer, kept the district moving. Jim’s contribution centered on entertainment: giving people a reason to come downtown, and a reason to come back. [1] [3]

The Haunted Warehouse, O’Brien’s, venues, and festivals became chapters in that effort. Reporting in 2020 describes Brent and Brett carrying the family’s business forward. [4]

JIM IN THE PUBLIC RECORD

The story Steve Lackmeyer told.

02 / THROUGH THE YEARS

THE YEARS THAT
BUILT THE STORY.

From Jim’s early businesses to a new life for old warehouses—and the family carrying that work forward. 27 milestones, with the people and places behind them.

BEFORE BRICKTOWN

These early chapters follow the family-supplied chronology of Steve Lackmeyer’s June 2008 profile. Approximate dates are marked.

1937

Where it all began

Jim D. Brewer is born February 6. His mother, Evelyn, raises him and his four sisters in southeast Oklahoma City by ironing clothes and sewing quilts. Jim is mowing lawns and doing odd jobs while still in grade school. [17]

c. 1948

Out on his own at 11

Jim leaves home to live with his grandfather near SE 28 and Central. He works until midnight at the Play More Bowling Alley at NW 4 and Broadway, walks miles home, and sleeps in the chicken coop so he doesn't break his grandfather's 5 a.m. breakfast rule. [17]

1950s–60s

Jim Dandy's Transmissions

Working at an uncle's salvage yard, Jim learns to rebuild transmissions. After marrying and starting a family, he opens his own shop, Jim Dandy's Transmissions, on Reno near Harvey. [18]

1960s–70s

The Superrig

Jim backs an acquaintance who wants to buy a nightclub, then takes it over when his partner can't run it. He finds he loves the business and greets every guest at the door. [18]

Late 1970s

Striking oil

Like much of Oklahoma during the boom, Jim buys an oil well. The first is a bust, but the second does very well. [18]

Early 1980s

The Tom Cat well

Jim’s recollection describes the Tom Cat well in western Oklahoma bringing in $600,000 in a single day. He leaves the nightclub life, sells his oil interests near the peak, and buys workover rigs, staying profitable through the subsequent oil downturn. [18]

Mid-1980s

Called to Bricktown

Looking for someone to carry on founding developer Neal Horton's work, his partner Williams turns to Jim for his cash and toughness. Jim starts buying warehouses from banks eager to sell. [19]

A DISTRICT COMES ALIVE
1985

A warehouse becomes a destination

Jim and Craig Brown see an opportunity in an old warehouse. The Bricktown Haunted Warehouse opens, giving people a reason to visit a district still finding its new identity. [1] [3]

1989

Restaurants bring new momentum

Spaghetti Warehouse opens. Its crowds help establish demand for dining and entertainment among Bricktown’s old buildings. [3]

1990

O’Brien’s & St. Patrick’s Day

Brent recalls opening O’Brien’s on March 17 alongside the parade and the first parking-lot block party. The pub and the celebration become part of the family story. [4]

Family recollection: Patsy sold T-shirts at O’Brien’s.

1991

Brewer Entertainment takes shape

Jim starts Brewer Entertainment Inc., bringing venues and outdoor festivals into a growing entertainment business. [5]

1997

Planning the canal together

Lackmeyer and Jack Money report on the public-private partnership behind the MAPS canal project, including Jim’s involvement as a Bricktown property owner. The Oklahoman ↗

1998

A new chapter for the depot

Jim purchases the Santa Fe Depot. Restoration helps prepare the historic station for the return of passenger rail. [12]

1999

The canal opens. The crowds arrive.

The Bricktown Canal opens in July, and the Heartland Flyer brings passenger service back to the depot. Recollections of the Fourth of July describe more than 50,000 people gathering for fireworks. [12] [6]

2007

Red, White and Boom! on the River

Brewer Entertainment promotes a free, three-day Fourth of July celebration at Downtown Airpark, with the Oklahoma City Philharmonic and other performers. Contemporary coverage previews the planned event. Oklahoma Gazette ↗

2008

A summer soundtrack

Contemporary festival coverage previews Bricktown Blues & BBQ, with Marcia Ball, Bugs Henderson, and regional musicians. Live music remains part of the district’s summer identity. [8]

JIM’S STORY, IN HIS LIFETIME
2008

Jim tells the rest of his story

The Oklahoman’s June video profile and Lackmeyer’s June 29 articles explore Jim’s early life, career, and the different views of his role in Bricktown. The Oklahoman Video Archive ↗ The Oklahoman ↗

2008

Remembering Jim

Jim dies on November 11. Family remembrance and local reporting reflect on his life, his businesses, and his role in Bricktown’s renewal. [2] [5]

THE FAMILY CARRIES IT FORWARD
2009

A place in the Walk of Fame

Lackmeyer reports on Walk of Fame recognition for Bricktown’s early developers, including Jim. The district’s public record begins a new chapter of remembrance. The Oklahoman ↗

2013

The Haunted Warehouse at Chevy

A Brewer Entertainment announcement documents the attraction’s 28th annual season at the Chevy Bricktown Events Center on California Avenue. [11]

2014

Another chapter for the event center

Lackmeyer reports on planned Chevy Bricktown Events Center renovations aimed at attracting performers. The venue remains part of the family’s entertainment story. The Oklahoman ↗

2014

Reggae Fest becomes a tradition

The Journal Record reports that Brewer Entertainment has hosted Reggae Fest for 19 years. The free festival brings performers and crowds together, alongside the practical challenges of producing outdoor events. [9]

2015

Renovating in Jim’s honor

The Journal Record covers Brent and Brett’s plans to bring new life to the former Haunted Warehouse buildings as a tribute to their father. The Journal Record ↗

2016

A new landmark on a familiar wall

Jack Fowler’s Bricktown Okctopus mural takes shape on the event-center wall. The large artwork becomes another recognizable part of the district. [14]

2019

New events. A continuing tradition.

Lackmeyer’s Bricktown Throwdown coverage connects the athletic competition to Brett and Brent’s event business and the district’s tradition of bringing people together. The Oklahoman ↗

2019

The sons carry the story forward

A November Lackmeyer feature follows Brent and Brett continuing to develop and invest in the places associated with their father’s legacy. The Oklahoman ↗

2020

Thirty years of St. Patrick’s Day

A Gazette interview recalls O’Brien’s 1990 opening and three decades of block parties. Brent describes the brothers’ continuing work and plans to dedicate that year’s celebration to Jim. [4]

Dates mark documented milestones and contemporary reporting. Plans and festival previews describe what was announced at the time. Family recollections are identified alongside published sources.

03 / COMPANIES, PLACES & TRADITIONS

THE COMPANIES.
THE PLACES. THE STORIES.

From Jim’s early businesses to the companies and venues that helped shape Bricktown.

16 stories

BEFORE BRICKTOWN

Jim Dandy’s Transmissions

A business story that began with hard work.

Before the downtown buildings and festival crowds, Jim ran Jim Dandy’s Transmissions. A 2020 Oklahoma Gazette account names the transmission business among his early ventures, alongside four nightclubs in the 1970s. It is an early chapter in the entrepreneurial path that eventually led to Bricktown. [4]

BEFORE BRICKTOWN · DATES APPROXIMATE

Super Rig Club

The Superrig. A doorway into nightlife.

The family’s chronology of Lackmeyer’s early-career profile recalls Jim backing an acquaintance’s nightclub, then taking over its operation. He discovered he enjoyed the business and welcomed guests at the door—a chapter that helped lead toward his later entertainment ventures. [18]

Also remembered as “The Superrig.” Exact opening and closing dates remain to be established.

THE FAMILY BUSINESS

Brewer Enterprises

Another name behind the Bricktown years.

Oklahoma Gazette’s November 2008 remembrance identifies Jim as the owner of both Brewer Enterprises and Brewer Entertainment. Brewer Enterprises deserves its own place in the family history; the report does not establish its founding date or a separate inventory of its assets. [6]

PROPERTY & DEVELOPMENT

Bricktown Real Estate

The buildings behind the possibilities.

Downtown OKC’s board directory lists Brent Brewer with Bricktown Real Estate LLC. An earlier Greater Oklahoma City Chamber report identifies Bricktown Real Estate as the Santa Fe Depot’s owner and Brent as its president. Together, those records document another company in the family’s downtown story. [15] [16]

THE ENTERTAINMENT YEARS

Bricktown Live

A venue with a chapter of its own.

The Journal Record’s 2008 remembrance lists Bricktown Live among the properties purchased and managed by Brewer Entertainment. Oklahoma Gazette also names it among the venues operated by Jim’s businesses. These are historical accounts; the exact opening and closing dates remain to be established. [5] [6]

THE ENTERTAINMENT YEARS

Bricktown Ballroom

Another place to bring people together.

Bricktown Ballroom appears in both The Journal Record and Oklahoma Gazette’s 2008 accounts of the Brewer venue portfolio. It belongs alongside Bricktown Live and the event center in the entertainment history. These sources establish the Brewer connection, while its full operating timeline remains to be documented. [5] [6]

1985

Bricktown Haunted Warehouse

The attraction that helped start it all.

The Haunted Warehouse gave people a reason to visit Bricktown before the canal and ballpark. Retro Metro OKC traces its origins to Jim Brewer and Craig Brown seeing possibilities in the old Hunzicker Lighting building. A 2013 Brewer Entertainment release documents its later home at the Chevy Bricktown Events Center. [1] [3] [11]

1990

O’Brien’s Bricktown Club

An Irish pub. A new Bricktown tradition.

In a 2020 interview, Brent Brewer recalled opening O’Brien’s on March 17, 1990, alongside the St. Patrick’s Day parade and a block party in the parking lot. He said the pub operated for seven years. The celebration outlived the venue and became part of the family’s continuing story. [4]

1991

Brewer Entertainment

Turning places into experiences.

The Journal Record’s 2008 remembrance dates Brewer Entertainment Inc.’s start to 1991. At that time, it described a portfolio that included the Coca-Cola Bricktown Events Center, Bricktown Live, Bricktown Ballroom, and the Santa Fe train depot, alongside outdoor festivals. [5]

FAMILY BUSINESS

Bricktown Parking

The practical side of welcoming a crowd.

Bricktown Parking belongs in the company history identified by the Brewer family. Public records also show why parking mattered to the district’s growth: the city’s 2008 parking strategy lists Jim Brewer among consulted stakeholders and Bricktown Parking Investors among contacted operators. [13]

About this chapter’s dates and records

The company’s founding date and the relationship between the differently named parking entities remain to be documented.

SUMMER TRADITION

Fourth of July festivals

Fireworks, music, and a city coming together.

A 2008 Oklahoma Gazette remembrance recounts the crowds at Bricktown’s 1999 Fourth of July fireworks after the canal opened. In 2007, the Gazette separately documented Brewer Entertainment’s Red, White and Boom! on the River—a free, three-day celebration at Downtown Airpark with the Oklahoma City Philharmonic and other performers. [6] [7]

BLUES & BBQ

Bricktown Blues Fest

A soundtrack for summer in Bricktown.

The 2008 Gazette preview documents a two-day, free Blues & BBQ festival at Sheridan and Oklahoma avenues, with Marcia Ball, Bugs Henderson, and regional musicians. The family identifies Blues Fest as part of its history; the public account establishes the festival and lineup. [8]

About this chapter’s dates and records

An original program or company archive will help document the first year and full production credits.

REGGAE & COMMUNITY

Bricktown Reggae Fest

A different rhythm for downtown.

The Journal Record reported in July 2014 that Brewer Entertainment had hosted Reggae Fest for 19 years. Its account describes a free event with performers including Watusi, Ugly Lion, and The Effinays, and an emphasis on bringing live entertainment to Bricktown. [9]

THE EVENT-CENTER YEARS

Coca-Cola & Chevy Bricktown Events Center

Two names in one venue’s story.

A 2008 account places the Coca-Cola venue within Brewer Entertainment’s operations. Songkick identifies Chevy Bricktown Event Center as formerly the Coca-Cola Bricktown Event Center. Brewer Entertainment’s 2013 announcement documents the Chevy name and a Haunted Warehouse season at the venue. [5] [10] [11]

About this chapter’s dates and records

The precise sponsorship-change date is still to be established.

1998

Santa Fe Depot

Preserving a gateway to Oklahoma City.

Amtrak’s station history records Jim Brewer’s 1998 purchase of the depot and the renovation that followed. The Heartland Flyer began service in 1999. This chapter connects the family’s downtown work with the return of passenger rail to Oklahoma. [12]

2016

The Bricktown Okctopus

A new landmark on a familiar wall.

Oklahoma Tourism records Jack Fowler’s mural on the north side of the Chevy Bricktown Events Center in late 2016. The 200-foot-wide artwork made the building part of Bricktown’s public-art landscape. [14]
